records.name: Banana Slug
records.diet: fallen leaves, mushrooms, animal droppings and other decaying matter; occasionally live seedlings
records.shelter: Under logs and loose bark; seals itself into a mucus cocoon and waits out dry spells
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, shaded forest floor that stays damp — deep leaf litter, mossy logs and seeps
records.fact: Banana slug slime is a numbing agent — one lick and most animals spit the slug straight back out, tongue tingling.
records.role: The banana slug is the forest floor's shredder. Fungi and bacteria do the fine chemistry; the slug does the chewing, grinding fallen leaves into wet crumbs that rot far faster and turning a whole autumn of leaves into soft duff. It grazes mushrooms too, and spores ride safely through its gut, so every silver trail plants fungi somewhere new. Gartersnakes and raccoons are two of the very few animals willing to put up with the slime.

requirements.hint: Deep damp leaves, mossy shade and mushrooms to graze. Skip the pond — this one drinks through its skin, straight out of the litter.

records.name: Tree Squirrel
records.diet: acorns, hickory nuts, tree buds, samaras and fungi; occasional insects and bird eggs
records.shelter: Tree cavity dens in winter and leaf-and-twig dreys built high in the canopy in summer
records.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous or mixed forest rich in oaks and hickories
records.fact: A squirrel buries thousands of nuts a year and forgets a good share of them. The forgotten ones grow into trees, so most squirrels accidentally plant a forest in a lifetime.
records.role: The gray squirrel is a seed eater who keeps failing at his own plan, and the woods are better for it: acorns buried and never dug up again are how oaks climb hills and fill gaps. Its droppings scatter fungal spores, its leafy summer dreys get taken over by great horned owls, and being the commonest mid-sized animal in the forest it is on the menu of nearly every predator here.

requirements.hint: Oaks to feed and bury from, a high fork for a summer drey, and a big tree to den in over winter.

sources.name: NC Wildlife Resources Commission — Eastern Gray Squirrel

records.name: Chipmunk
records.diet: seeds, acorns, hickory nuts, berries and underground fungi, plus some insects and bird eggs
records.shelter: Underground burrows up to 10 m long with a nest chamber and a seed-storage larder
records.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous forest with logs, stumps and diggable soil
records.fact: A chipmunk can cram so many acorns into its cheek pouches that its head looks twice as wide, then unload them into an underground pantry holding more than a litre of seeds. It wakes up all winter to snack — chipmunks never truly hibernate.
records.role: The chipmunk is a hoarder and a digger. Every seed it carries off and never eats is a seed planted somewhere new, and spores from the fungi it digs up travel with it. Its tunnels loosen and air the soil. Small, common and awake in daylight, it is the prey base almost every predator here is waiting on — which is why so many of them cannot come back until it does.

requirements.hint: A brush pile to bolt into is enough to start with.

records.name: Porcupine
records.diet: almost entirely herbivorous — inner bark in winter, buds, twigs and leaves in summer — but gnaws shed antlers and bones for minerals
records.shelter: Rock dens and hollow logs, reused season after season; also rests high in tree canopies
records.preferredHabitat: Mixed and coniferous forest with thick-barked trees, especially hemlock, and rock or log dens below
records.fact: A porcupine cannot throw its quills — they simply stick to whatever bumps them. The barbed tips are coated in a natural antibiotic, so a porcupine that falls out of a tree and lands on itself usually heals up fine.
records.role: Porcupines improve the forest by damaging it. Stripping bark kills limbs and whole trees, and those dying trees become the snags, loose bark slabs and cavities that woodpeckers, bats and denning mammals move into — one animal's dinner is another animal's house. They eat the same nuts as squirrels and elk, and they are the entire reason a fisher would bother living here.

requirements.hint: Hemlock and pine bark to live on through winter, and a hollow log or rock den to sleep the day away in.

records.name: Woodpecker
records.diet: mostly insects — beetle larvae, ants, caterpillars — with some berries and sap
records.shelter: Excavates its own cavity in a small dead stub, usually in wood already softened by fungus; roosts in cavities year-round
records.preferredHabitat: Open deciduous and mixed woodland with small dead stubs and dead limbs on living trees
records.fact: A downy woodpecker weighs about as much as four sheets of paper — light enough to hang off a dead weed stem and drill into it, which no bigger woodpecker can manage.
records.role: The downy cuts the small holes. It can only chisel wood that fungi have already softened, so it waits on the decomposers — and the nuthatches and chickadees, which cannot cut a hole at all, wait on it. It works bark crevices and dead twigs for beetle grubs and ants that heavier woodpeckers can't reach, and its eggs feed climbing snakes.

requirements.hint: Small dead stubs with the wood already gone soft. It cannot chisel healthy timber, so leave the rotting stuff standing.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Downy Woodpecker life history

records.name: Nuthatch
records.diet: insects and spiders from bark in summer; acorns, hickory nuts and cached seeds through winter
records.shelter: Natural cavities and old woodpecker holes in mature hardwoods; cannot excavate its own
records.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous and mixed forest with large oaks and hickories
records.fact: A nuthatch walks down tree trunks head-first, which lets it spot insects tucked in bark that every upward-climbing bird walks straight past.
records.role: The nuthatch reads the bark upside down, taking beetles, insect eggs and spiders from angles other birds never see. In autumn it wedges acorns and seeds into bark cracks to hammer open later, shifting seed around the woods. It cannot cut a hole of its own, so it moves into last year's downy woodpecker hole — no woodpecker, no nuthatch.

requirements.hint: An old woodpecker hole it can move straight into, with big oaks to work over and stash seeds in.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — White-breasted Nuthatch

records.name: Forest Salamander
records.diet: small invertebrates: mites, springtails, spiders, beetles, ants and earthworms
records.shelter: Under logs, bark and damp leaf litter; lays its eggs in a cavity inside rotting wood and stays coiled around them
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp deciduous forest floor with abundant rotting wood — and no pond required anywhere in its life
records.fact: Add up all the red-backed salamanders in a patch of forest and they can outweigh every bird in it. They have no lungs at all — the whole animal breathes through its skin.
records.role: This salamander is the bridge between the leaf litter and everything above it: it eats the mites, springtails and small worms that shred fallen leaves, and its own huge numbers feed snakes, birds and small mammals. It also breaks the rule everyone learns about amphibians — no pond, no tadpole, the entire life cycle inside one rotting log. Skin-breathing means it dries out fast, so the ground has to stay damp.

requirements.hint: This one skips the tadpole stage completely — the eggs hatch fully formed inside a rotting log. No pond needed, just damp wood and deep leaves.

sources.name: Virginia Herpetological Society — Eastern Red-backed Salamander

records.name: Raccoon
records.diet: opportunistic: crayfish, insects, earthworms, frogs, eggs and fruit, with vertebrate prey a smaller share than most people assume
records.shelter: Hollow tree dens preferred; also rock crevices, burrows and buildings
records.preferredHabitat: Moist forest beside water shallow enough to wade and feel around in
records.fact: A raccoon sees with its hands. Its front paws carry four to five times more touch nerves than most mammals', and it will stare off in the opposite direction while its fingers read a stream bed.
records.role: The raccoon carries the stream into the woods: it feels out crayfish and insects in the shallows and unloads that energy up the bank, dropping fruit seeds as it goes. It is also this forest's great nest robber — the same crowd of cavities that lets wood ducks and flying squirrels move in hands a raccoon a list of doors to try.

requirements.hint: A hollow den log and a stony shallow edge to feel around in. It hunts with its hands, not its eyes.

records.name: Black Bear
records.diet: berries, acorns and nuts above all; also grasses and forbs, insects and grubs, carrion, and fawns in spring
records.shelter: Winter dens under upturned root masses, in hollow trees and rock cavities, or dug into a bank
records.preferredHabitat: Dense forest with a thick understory and reliable berry and acorn crops
records.fact: Black bear cubs are born in the middle of hibernation, blind and smaller than a soup can, and their mother barely wakes up for it.
records.role: A black bear ties the whole forest together in one animal: berries, acorns, grubs torn out of rotting logs, an elk calf in spring. It carries berry seeds for miles before dropping them, and every log it rips apart rots faster afterwards. A bear's year is really an acorn year — when the mast crop fails bears wander enormous distances, and a forest with no oaks cannot keep them. Nothing here hunts a grown bear.

requirements.hint: A full larder and a winter bed: heavy berry crops, acorn-bearing oaks, water, and a den under the tipped-up roots of a fallen tree.

records.name: Gray Fox
records.diet: mice, voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds and eggs — and in late summer an astonishing amount of fruit
records.shelter: Hollow logs, rock crevices and old earth dens; it will also curl up on a branch well off the ground
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy woodland edges and old clearings growing back, with tangled climbable cover
records.fact: It is the only dog in the world that climbs trees. A gray fox hooks its curved claws into the bark, shins up the trunk like a cat, and naps ten metres up where nothing that hunts it can follow.
records.role: The forest's climbing fox. It works the brushy edges for mice, rabbits and ground-nesting birds, then goes straight up a trunk after squirrels, nests and grapes. By late summer it is eating so much fruit that its droppings are half seeds, which plants the next generation of berry tangles all along the edge. Bobcats kill it when they catch it in the open and great horned owls take its kits, so it keeps a climbable tree within a sprint at all times.

requirements.hint: A brushy edge to hunt along, a dry bank to den in, and something woody to climb — going straight up a trunk is how this one gets away from whatever is bigger. Fruit matters as much as mice here.

records.name: Ratsnake
records.diet: mice, voles, chipmunks and young squirrels, plus birds and eggs lifted straight out of nests
records.shelter: Hollow trunks, rot pockets and stump cavities; the eggs go into a warm heap of rotting wood chips
records.preferredHabitat: Old woods and woodland edges with big rough-barked trees to climb and rodents underneath them
records.fact: A ratsnake can climb straight up a bare tree trunk with nothing to hold onto. It wedges the edges of its belly scales into the ridges in the bark and walks up the side of the tree, then robs the nest at the top.
records.role: The forest's rodent brake, and the only hunter here that works in three dimensions. On the ground it takes mice, voles and chipmunks by the dozen; up in the canopy it raids old woodpecker holes and songbird nests, which is why every bird in earshot mobs it. It kills by wrapping and squeezing, not venom, and when it is startled it freezes into a stiff kinked shape that looks exactly like a fallen branch. She never sits on her eggs — she buries them in rotting wood and lets the heat of the rot do the incubating. Foxes, fishers and great horned owls eat it.

requirements.hint: Big rough-barked trees are the whole trick — this snake hunts up them as much as under them. Leave a heap of rotting wood chips at the foot of a stump for her eggs, and skip the pond; she does not need one.

records.name: Bobcat
records.diet: obligate carnivore: rabbits, squirrels and rodents, plus some birds, reptiles and deer fawns
records.shelter: Dens under rock ledges, in hollow logs and in dense thickets; a female moves her kittens if disturbed
records.preferredHabitat: Forest with a dense understory, brushy edges and broken rocky ground
records.fact: A bobcat can bring down prey eight times its own weight, then bury the leftovers under leaves or snow and come back the next night.
records.role: With no wolves or cougars in these woods, the bobcat is the top hunter on the ground and nothing hunts a grown one. It takes everything from chipmunks up to raccoons, foxes and even fishers, and it kills by ambush — creeping close through cover, then one short rush. Strip the understory and the bobcat leaves, however much prey is still standing around: it has nothing left to hide behind.

requirements.hint: Dense understory to stalk through, a sheltered rock den for kittens, and plenty of prey already back.

records.name: Great Horned Owl
records.diet: mammals and birds — rabbits, skunks, even other owls — plus frogs
records.shelter: Never builds a nest: takes over an old hawk, crow or squirrel nest, or a broken snag top or ledge
records.preferredHabitat: Mature forest broken by open ground, with big trees holding other animals' abandoned nests
records.fact: Great horned owls are one of the only animals that regularly kill and eat skunks. The spray does not appear to bother them in the slightest.
records.role: The great horned owl runs the night shift and eats a longer list of animals than any other bird of prey here — squirrels, bats, snakes, ducks, even porcupines — and adults have nothing above them. It builds nothing at all: it starts nesting in midwinter by claiming an old squirrel drey or hawk nest somebody else made last spring, which is why the squirrels have to come back before the owl can.

requirements.hint: Tall trees holding somebody else's old nest — this one never builds its own — and prey already back in the woods.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Great Horned Owl life history

records.name: Grasshopper
records.diet: grasses, sedges and broadleaf forbs
records.shelter: Shelters down in grass and low vegetation; lays eggs in firm bare soil
records.preferredHabitat: Sunny grasslands and meadows rich in grasses and forbs
records.fact: A grasshopper's ears are on its belly — a pair of eardrums on the first segment of the abdomen, nowhere near its head.
records.role: Grasshoppers turn grass into food for everything else. Almost every meat-eater in this meadow takes them at some point — birds, snakes, foxes, spiders, mantises, even a screech owl — so a good grasshopper summer is a good summer for the whole food web.

requirements.hint: They return almost as soon as the grass does.

records.name: Prairie Vole
records.diet: grasses, sedges, seeds and roots, plus bark in winter
records.shelter: Shallow burrows and woven grass nests linked by clipped surface runways
records.preferredHabitat: Dense grassy prairie and meadow with thick ground cover left standing
records.fact: Prairie voles pair up and stay together, and both parents raise the pups — which is why scientists who study bonding and loyalty end up studying this small brown rodent.
records.role: The vole is the meadow's engine of small furry food. It mows narrow highways through the grass, breeds fast, and feeds hawks, owls, foxes, coyotes, snakes and badgers. The burrows it abandons get taken over by bumble bee queens and garter snakes, so it builds homes as well as filling stomachs.

requirements.hint: Thick unmown grass with clipped runways beneath it. This one arrives early, and almost everything with teeth or talons is waiting on it.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Microtus ochrogaster

records.name: Monarch Butterfly
records.diet: caterpillars eat only milkweed; adults sip flower nectar
records.shelter: Roosts in trees and shrubs; overwinters clustered in dense groves far to the south
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and roadsides with milkweed to breed on and nectar flowers to refuel on
records.fact: No single monarch flies the whole round trip. The butterflies that head south in autumn are the great-grandchildren of the ones that came north in spring, and they find the same groves anyway.
records.role: Monarch caterpillars eat milkweed and store its poison in their own bodies, so a bird that tries one usually spits it out and remembers the orange for the rest of its life. It doesn't save them from everything — mantises, spiders, wasps and ants take eggs and caterpillars by the thousand, and only a few in every hundred ever grow wings.

requirements.hint: A spreading milkweed bed for the caterpillars — nothing else will do — and nectar flowers close by for the adults.

records.name: Bumblebee
records.diet: nectar for fuel and pollen for protein, from a wide range of flowers
records.shelter: Nests in abandoned rodent burrows, grass tussocks and ground cavities
records.preferredHabitat: Flower-rich meadows with something in bloom from spring to frost
records.fact: Some flowers refuse to let go of their pollen unless they are shaken. A bumblebee grabs on and buzzes its flight muscles until the pollen falls out — tomatoes and blueberries depend on it.
records.role: Big, furry and warm enough to fly on cold grey mornings when other bees are still grounded, the bumblebee is the meadow's heavy-duty pollinator. A whole colony starts with one queen in spring hunting for an old vole hole to move into, so nest holes matter every bit as much as flowers. Orb weavers and crab spiders take her at the flowers, and badgers dig entire nests out of the ground.

requirements.hint: Flowers are only half of it. A queen also needs an abandoned vole hole under a thick grass tussock to start her colony in.

records.name: Cottontail Rabbit
records.diet: grasses and clover in summer; twigs, bark and buds in winter
records.shelter: Rests in shallow grass 'forms'; bolts into brush piles and old burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and field edges with brushy cover close enough to run to
records.fact: A cottontail doesn't dig a burrow. It presses a shallow bowl into the grass called a form and sits so still in it that you can walk straight past.
records.role: Cottontails eat grass and clover all summer and switch to twigs and bark in winter, and they breed fast enough to keep up with everything that hunts them — fox, coyote, badger, hawk and owl all count on them. Their droppings feed the soil life underfoot, which is a polite way of saying rabbits fertilise the meadow they eat.

requirements.hint: A brushy form to bolt into, native grass to graze, and berries close by. It gets most of its water straight out of green plants.

records.name: Mule Deer
records.diet: shrubs, forbs, twigs and buds, plus grasses in spring
records.shelter: Beds down in brushy cover or tall grass; no permanent den
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and shrubby edges with browse and daily water
records.fact: A bounding mule deer lands on all four hooves at once like a pogo stick, and puffs out scent from a gland on its hind leg as it goes — a warning the other deer can smell.
records.role: The mule deer is a browser rather than a grazer: it works on shrub twigs, buds and broad-leaved plants instead of cropping turf, so it shapes the edges of the meadow rather than the middle. Its browsing and droppings move nutrients around. Coyotes take fawns; a healthy adult is more than most hunters here want to take on.

requirements.hint: Real browse — serviceberry twigs and buds, not lawn — plus water it can reach every day.

records.name: Ladybug
records.diet: aphids and other small soft-bodied insects, as both larva and adult
records.shelter: Overwinters packed into leaf litter in big huddles; shelters on foliage in summer
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows with aphid-bearing plants, especially milkweed
records.fact: One ladybug can put away around 5,000 aphids in a lifetime. Pinch it and it bleeds bitter yellow blood out of its knees, which is why most birds spit it straight back out.
records.role: Larva and adult both hunt aphids, so a ladybug's whole life runs on an aphid supply — in this meadow, the yellow oleander aphids crowding the milkweed stems. Its bright shell is a warning label and it works on most birds. Mantises and orb weavers are not most birds.

requirements.hint: A patch of clover. The aphids arrive on their own, and that is the whole invitation.

records.name: Ground Squirrel
records.diet: mostly seeds, grasses, flowers and fungi, plus insects like grasshoppers
records.shelter: Big multi-entrance burrow systems dug into deep open ground
records.preferredHabitat: Open grassy meadow and slopes with a stone wall or bank to keep watch from
records.fact: Facing a rattlesnake, this squirrel kicks sand and waves its tail — and pumps hot blood into the tail first, so the snake's heat-sensing pits see a far bigger animal than is really standing there.
records.role: A digger and a generalist. It eats seeds, greens, fungi and insects, turns over soil every time it excavates, and the tunnels it abandons become homes for bumble bee queens, garter snakes and foxes. Its colonies are what pull badgers, hawks and coyotes into a meadow in the first place.

requirements.hint: Deep diggable soil for a burrow town, and a stone wall to stand sentry on.

sources.name: PNAS — infrared tail-flagging in ground squirrels

records.name: Western Meadowlark
records.diet: mostly insects in summer — beetles, grasshoppers, crickets — and seeds in winter
records.shelter: A domed grass nest woven on the ground, usually with a covered runway leading in
records.preferredHabitat: Wide native grassland with song perches and no shrubs moving in
records.fact: A meadowlark weaves a roof over its nest and a covered tunnel leading in, so from above there is nothing to see at all — just grass.
records.role: A grassland bird through and through. It eats grasshoppers, crickets and beetles by the hundred all summer and switches to seed in winter, and it needs real open space — as shrubs and trees creep in, meadowlarks quietly vanish. A plump bird that nests on the ground is a favourite of hawks, foxes, badgers and coyotes.

requirements.hint: Wide unbroken native grass and a perch to sing from. Skip the shrubs here — woody cover is exactly what pushes this one out.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Western Meadowlark

records.name: Garter Snake
records.diet: earthworms, pillbugs, amphibians, slugs, insects and young rodents
records.shelter: Shelters under stone walls and logs; winters below the frost line in a communal den
records.preferredHabitat: Moist meadow and grassland near sunny stones and water
records.fact: Garter snakes spend the whole winter piled together by the dozen in one frost-free hole underground, and come pouring back out of it in a knot in spring.
records.role: The meadow's damp-grass hunter — earthworms, pillbugs, frogs, insects and young voles, always within reach of water. It is harmless to people, though a bite can itch. Where it can survive the winter is what decides where it can live at all, so one deep frost-free den matters more than anything else you can build for it.

requirements.hint: Water to hunt beside, warm stone to bask on, and a den deep enough to spend the winter below the frost.

records.name: Red Fox
records.diet: voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds and insects, rounded out with berries and carrion
records.shelter: Enlarges a burrow another animal dug into a natal den; also uses brush and hollows
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows, field edges and hedgerows across open country
records.fact: A fox listening for a vole under deep grass or snow lines itself up facing magnetic north before it leaps — and the trick only seems to help when it cannot see the prey at all.
records.role: A stalk-and-pounce generalist that keeps rodent and rabbit numbers down and fills the gaps with insects, berries and whatever it finds already dead. It rarely digs a den from scratch — it widens an old ground squirrel or badger burrow instead. Great horned owls take its kits, and now that coyotes are back, foxes have to give ground.

requirements.hint: This one comes back once the small animals do — and she needs an old burrow she can widen into a nursery.

sources.name: Phys.org — magnetic alignment in fox predation (Cerveny et al.)

records.name: Red-tailed Hawk
records.diet: mostly small mammals — voles, ground squirrels, rabbits — plus birds and snakes
records.shelter: A bulky stick nest in the crown of a tall tree or on a cliff ledge
records.preferredHabitat: Open country seen from above: grassland, fields and meadows
records.fact: That screaming eagle cry in every film is a red-tailed hawk. Actual bald eagles sound like squeaky gulls, so the movies quietly swapped them.
records.role: The daylight hunter over this meadow, either circling on broad flat wings or sitting on a pole staring at the grass. It is heavy and powerful and built for taking prey off the ground — voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, snakes — not for chasing birds through the air. The huge stick nest it builds gets inherited by a great horned owl the very next winter.

requirements.hint: A tall tree crown for the stick nest, open grass to hunt over, and a meadow already full of small mammals. It takes its water from its prey.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Red-tailed Hawk

records.name: Minnow
records.diet: algae, diatoms and plankton sifted off mud, stems and stones, plus detritus and small insect larvae.
records.shelter: Reed roots, submerged plant beds, and the shaded underside of sunken wood.
records.preferredHabitat: Connected, clean, weedy pools.
records.fact: The male minnow scrubs the underside of a sunken slab spotless using a spongy pad on his own back, then guards the eggs the females glue to that ceiling — fanning them day and night until they hatch.
records.role: The little silver engine of the marsh. Minnow schools graze algae and plankton and then get eaten by nearly everything with a bill, a beak or a claw — and they give baby mussels a free ride to new water on their gills.

requirements.hint: Clean pools that join up to each other, plus something flat and submerged for the males to glue their eggs underneath.

sources.name: Missouri Department of Conservation — Fathead Minnow

records.name: Beaver
records.diet: bark and cambium of willow and aspen, plus cattail rhizomes and submerged plants
records.shelter: Stick-and-mud lodges with underwater entrances
records.preferredHabitat: Slow channels with mud banks and woody plants to fell
records.fact: A beaver's front teeth never stop growing and are orange because they are reinforced with iron — living chisels that gnawing keeps sharp. Its lips shut behind those teeth, so it can carry and cut branches underwater without swallowing the pond.
records.role: The marsh's engineer, and the turning point of the whole restoration. Fell a few willows, dam a channel, and suddenly there is deep permanent water with drowned trees standing in it — the pond the otter, the merganser, the kingfisher, the heron and the eagle all move in on afterwards.

requirements.hint: Willows to fell and eat, a soft bank to den in, and enough water to float a log. Once it settles, seven new habitats become buildable.

sources.name: US Forest Service — Beaver as ecosystem engineers

records.name: Muskrat
records.diet: mainly cattails, bulrush and roots; sometimes freshwater mussels and small fish
records.shelter: Dome lodges woven from cattail and reed, and burrows dug into banks
records.preferredHabitat: Reedy shallows with abundant cattails
records.fact: A muskrat can stay under for a quarter of an hour on one breath, and in midwinter it dives beneath the ice to dig up frozen-in cattail roots and eat them down there in the dark.
records.role: The cattail harvester. It clips reeds into lodges and feeding lanes that ducks and herons then hunt along, it feeds the mink, the otter and the eagle, and the bank burrows it abandons are the only homes mink ever move into.

requirements.hint: Cattails to eat and to build lodges from, and shallow water over their roots so it can keep feeding all winter.

records.name: Mallard
records.diet: mostly seeds and submerged plants, though hens switch to insect larvae, snails and freshwater shrimp while laying, and ducklings eat almost nothing else at first
records.shelter: Ground nests hidden in dense sedge and grass tussocks near water
records.preferredHabitat: Calm, plant-rich shallows with tussock cover on the bank
records.fact: Mallards sleep with one eye open and half the brain awake. On a raft of sleeping ducks it is the ones on the outside doing the watching — and they swap places so everyone gets a proper nap.
records.role: The tail-up dabbler of the shallows, tipping forward to reach seeds and leaves it can't dive for. Hens switch to insects and snails while they are laying, and ducklings eat almost nothing else at first, so a mallard family needs a bug-rich marsh, not just a weedy one.

requirements.hint: Water shallow enough to tip into headfirst, and thick dry tussocks a few steps up the bank for the hen to hide her nest in.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Mallard life history

records.name: Painted Turtle
records.diet: mostly aquatic plants and algae as an adult; hatchlings and young turtles eat far more insects and carrion
records.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; hauls out onto logs to bask
records.preferredHabitat: Still water with basking logs
records.fact: A painted turtle spends the entire winter under the ice without taking a breath. It absorbs what oxygen it can through its back end, and when that runs short it dissolves minerals out of its own shell to stay alive until spring.
records.role: The marsh's sunbather. A cold turtle cannot digest a thing, so a log in the sun is a feeding requirement rather than a luxury — and as painted turtles grow they flip from hunting insects to grazing plants.

requirements.hint: Still water, a soft mud bottom, and a log tilted up out of the water. No sunny log, no digestion.

sources.name: Turtle Guardians — Butt breathers and frogsicles: overwintering herpetofauna

records.name: Red-winged Blackbird
records.diet: insects in summer, seeds and grain the rest of the year
records.shelter: Cup nests wound around several upright stems standing in water
records.preferredHabitat: Dense cattail and reed stands with water underneath
records.fact: A male red-wing can switch his scarlet shoulder patches on and off. Flared wide they start fights; tucked away under the black feathers they let him slip through a rival's territory completely unnoticed.
records.role: The loudest bird in the marsh and the first one back in spring. It hunts insects all summer and switches to seeds for the rest of the year, and it winds its nest around standing stems with water underneath — a moat the mink will not cross.

requirements.hint: Standing stems with water beneath them. The nest is stitched around the reeds and the water underneath is the burglar alarm.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Red-winged Blackbird life history

records.name: Sandhill Crane
records.diet: grains, tubers, insects, crayfish and small animals
records.shelter: Large ground mounds of piled marsh plants standing in shallow water
records.preferredHabitat: Broad, quiet, restored marshland
records.fact: Cranes dance to choose a partner — leaping, bowing and flinging sticks in the air — and once they pair up they usually stay together for life. Their bugling carries more than two kilometres because the windpipe is coiled up inside the breastbone like a trumpet.
records.role: The tallest bird on the marsh and the last one to arrive. Cranes probe the mud for tubers and snap up frogs, crayfish and insects, and they will only settle where the water is wide, quiet and genuinely healthy.

requirements.hint: This one wants space and quiet. Build a wide, well-balanced marsh and heap a nest mound up above the waterline.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Sandhill Crane life history

records.name: Chorus Frog
records.diet: small insects and other tiny invertebrates
records.shelter: Damp litter and loose bark under fallen wood in winter; wet vegetation in summer
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow pools ringed with reeds and wet meadow
records.fact: A chorus frog freezes solid every winter. Ice fills the spaces around its organs, its heart stops for weeks — and in spring it thaws out and starts singing as though nothing happened. The call sounds exactly like running your thumb along a comb.
records.role: Small enough to sit on a coin and loud enough to hear right across the marsh. It mops up tiny insects all summer and then feeds herons, mink, otters and cranes — the most-eaten voice in the wetland.

requirements.hint: Shallow water to sing and breed in, and a deep, damp pile of leaves on dry land to spend the winter frozen inside.

sources.name: Michigan Natural Features Inventory — Pseudacris maculata
Montana Field Guide — Boreal Chorus Frog

records.name: Tiger Salamander
records.diet: worms, insects, freshwater shrimp and other small invertebrates; larvae take tadpoles
records.shelter: Damp burrows in soft ground near fishless breeding pools
records.preferredHabitat: Fishless seasonal pools with soft banks
records.fact: Tiger salamanders spend most of their lives alone underground, then walk back on the first warm rainy night of spring to the exact pool they hatched in — and if that pool starts drying too fast, some larvae grow oversized heads and start eating their own brothers and sisters.
records.role: A fat, blotched, black-and-gold hunter that only breeds where fish cannot live. Its larvae race to grow legs before the pool dries, which is a bet they can only win in water no minnow could survive.

requirements.hint: Dig the vernal pools well away from the fish pools and let them dry right out in summer. Fish and it larvae cannot share water.

sources.name: US Fish & Wildlife Service — Eastern Tiger Salamander

records.name: Dragonfly
records.diet: flying insects as an adult; the underwater nymph takes midge larvae, freshwater shrimp, tadpoles and fish fry
records.shelter: Emergent reed stems for the adults; the nymphs live in the water below
records.preferredHabitat: Clean open water with emergent stems to climb out on
records.fact: Dragonflies catch about 95 out of every 100 things they chase — a better strike rate than a lion, a shark or a falcon. They also see the world in something close to slow motion, which is why swatting one never works.
records.role: A hunter with two completely different lives. The nymph spends a year underwater firing out a hinged, grabbing lower lip at tadpoles and fish fry; then it climbs a reed stem, splits its own back open and flies away to hunt mosquitoes over the marsh.

requirements.hint: Open, clean water for the nymphs below, and tall stems at the edge for them to climb when it is time to change.

sources.name: Natural History Museum — Dragonflies: the ultimate hunters

records.name: Mink
records.diet: fish, frogs, crayfish, muskrats, and the eggs and young of marsh birds
records.shelter: Bank burrows, usually taken over from muskrats rather than dug
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy banks beside busy water
records.fact: A mink will chase a fish thirty metres underwater, and it hunts on land, in the water and up trees. What it almost never does is dig — it simply moves into a burrow a muskrat made and does not ask.
records.role: A small brown fury with an enormous menu: fish, frogs, crayfish, muskrats, eggs, ducklings, whatever is slowest that day. Its home is always second-hand, so no muskrats usually means no mink no matter how much prey there is.

requirements.hint: Water to hunt in, and a bank den — but something else has to dig that den first.

records.name: Great Blue Heron
records.diet: fish, frogs, salamanders, crayfish and large insects
records.shelter: Colonial stick nests built high in tall trees and snags near water
records.preferredHabitat: Still shallows for slow, patient hunting, with tall nest trees within reach
records.fact: A heron's neck has one specially kinked bone in it that works like a loaded spring — the strike is over faster than you can blink, and the fish is caught crosswise in the bill rather than speared.
records.role: The tall grey statue of the shallows. It hunts alone but flatly refuses to nest alone, packing dozens of stick nests into one stand of tall trees — and it spends a good part of its life being chased and robbed of its catch by eagles.

requirements.hint: Shallow water full of fish and frogs, and a stand of tall trees for the colony. This one nests alongside its own kind or not at all.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Great Blue Heron life history
Audubon Field Guide — Great Blue Heron

records.name: River Otter
records.diet: fish, crayfish, mussels, frogs and other aquatic animals
records.shelter: Bank dens with underwater entrances — usually a beaver's old lodge or burrow
records.preferredHabitat: Clean, connected water rich in fish and slow prey
records.fact: An otter has around 350,000 hairs packed into every square centimetre of its fur — more than most animals have on their entire body. It is the air trapped in all that fur, not fat, that keeps an otter warm in freezing water.
records.role: The best swimmer in the marsh and the top hunter under the surface. Otters need a lot of clean connected water and a den they did not dig themselves, so an otter here means the beaver came back first — and it means the eagles finally have someone worth robbing.

requirements.hint: Lots of connected clean water, plenty of fish and crayfish, and an old beaver-made bank den with an underwater door.
